Here's the 5-sign check I use to see if your meetings are patching a data gap:

(Save this + repost if useful ♻️)

A diary tells me a lot about a structure. When numbers arrive late or disagree, people meet to settle it by talking. That is a system problem showing up as a calendar problem.

1. The same update gets given twice, once to the team and again to the leadership group.
2. Meetings open with "which version of the report are we using?"
3. Decisions wait for the next scheduled meeting because nobody trusts the live figure.
4. One person is invited to everything, because they hold context nobody wrote down.
5. Actions from last week get re-discussed, because nobody can see their status.

Score yourself. One tick is normal. Three or more means your people are spending hours each week doing the job a connected system should do for them.

The fix is rarely fewer meetings. It is a structure where the report is current, shared and owned, so the meeting can be about decisions instead of data. That is what I mean by a system that empowers your people.

Better numbers, better meetings, better use of your best people's time.

Which sign did you recognise first?
Comment: If you want to try this with your team, count the hours your leadership group spends in recurring meetings this month, then circle the ones where the first ten minutes go on reconciling numbers. That circle is your starting list.
P.S. Comment: P.S. Hours multiplied by hourly cost gives you the number worth taking to your next budget round.

We came to school on a Saturday, and nobody made us.

I was in Grade 11. A young teacher, only a few years older than us, loved computers so much he opened the school computer room every Saturday. We played, shared what we found, and taught each other hardware and software.

It grew into a computer club. We trained for programming competitions run by a leading IT university in Jakarta. We did not win.

But a team formed, and something else formed with it.

He never handed us the answer. He pointed us at the problem and said, in his own way, go and find out. Be curious. Keep going until it works for you.

I did not see what he had given me until much later. Learning how to learn is the best skill anyone can have. It carried me from that room into a computer science degree, a long run of certifications, and years later into enterprise architecture at IBM. He stayed a mentor well into my career, until around 2010.

Today I walk into mid-market firms and do what he taught me. I do not arrive with the answer. I get curious about their people, their process and their technology, until the whole structure makes sense.

There's no coincidence, everything has a reason. A Saturday in a school computer room was part of mine.

Who taught you how to learn?
Comment: Mine was a teacher who gave up his Saturdays. If someone did that for you, tag them or tell their story below. People like that rarely hear how far it went.
P.S. Comment: P.S. Curiosity is a skill you can practise, and it compounds like interest.

“We're covered, we have insurance.”

I hear this often, and I understand why. It is a sensible thing to hold. But insurance and resilience do two different jobs.

A policy can help with the repair bill after something fails. It does not give back the week your team could not invoice, the client who waited, or the confidence of the board after a bad incident.

For example, a failed server can be replaced and the cost recovered. The days of lost momentum stay lost.

Insurance responds after the event. Structure decides whether the event happens, how big it gets, and how quickly you are back to normal.

I learned this on enterprise systems, where the aim was never to be repaid well. The aim was to stay up. That is why I treat recovery time as a design choice, made early and tested, instead of a claim form filled in later.

Keep the policy. Then ask the next question: if our most important system stopped tonight, what would our structure do in the first hour?

Better prepared, better recovered, better protected.

How would your business answer that first-hour question today?
Comment: Curious which part of the first hour feels clearest in your business and which feels like a gap. Happy to hear it below.
P.S. Comment: P.S. Cover is the safety net. Structure is the reason you rarely need it.

Here's the 1-page decision record I would put in every mid-market firm:

(Save this + repost if useful ♻️)

Large enterprises write down why a structural decision was made. Most $20M firms keep it in someone's head. A single page fixes that, and it takes ten minutes.

1. Decision. One sentence on what was chosen.
2. Why now. The business problem it solves, in plain words.
3. Options considered. At least three, including doing nothing.
4. Fit check. How it touches your people, process, technology and risk.
5. Cost and ROI. What it costs, and what it returns in time or margin.
6. Owner. One named person who answers for it.

Here's the 30-minute recovery drill I would run with your leadership team this week:

(Save this + repost if useful ♻️)

A drill costs half an hour. It shows you what your structure does under pressure, while the pressure is still pretend.

1. Pick one scenario: your main system is down from 9am tomorrow.
2. Minutes 0 to 5. Each person writes who they would call first, without talking.
3. Compare the answers. Different names on the page is your first finding.
4. Minutes 5 to 15. Walk the first hour. Who decides, who tells clients, who keeps the books moving?
5. Minutes 15 to 25. List what you could not do, and for how many hours.
6. Minutes 25 to 30. Pick the single biggest gap and give it one owner and one date.

Do not fix anything in the room. The point is to see it.

Expect your first finding within minutes. Capable people often carry different pictures of the same plan. A drill puts those pictures side by side.

Run it once a quarter and the answers start to match. That is what a team that recovers fast looks like.

Good luck, and let the first drill be an easy one.

Which scenario would you pick first?
Comment: Tip for your first drill: choose a scenario that is realistic but not frightening, like a key system being unavailable for half a day. Easy wins build the habit.
P.S. Comment: P.S. Write the answers on a whiteboard, not a laptop. Everyone sees the same picture.

“Open-source is risky. Stick with the big names.”

I understand why people say it. Big names feel safe, and nobody gets blamed for choosing them.

But my first real lesson in infrastructure said otherwise. Early in my career, my manager taught me how to build it, on Microsoft and on open-source. When I saw what open-source could do, it blew my mind. In the right setting it can be as resilient as the paid option, and sometimes more resilient. People paid for it, and people were happy with it. The ROI was much better.

That does not make open-source always right. It makes fit the thing to test.

What worries me more is the opposite habit. Leaders buy a big name on the strength of the marketing, then use a small slice of what they pay for. Safe on paper, expensive in practice.

My test is simple. I ask whether the option suits your people, your process and your budget, and what it returns over three years. Sometimes the answer is open-source. Sometimes it is a subscription. Sometimes it is the big commercial platform.

Choose on fit, and the brand takes care of itself.

When did you last choose a system for fit instead of for the name?
Comment: Good tools come in all three kinds. What matters is that someone checked the fit before signing. Share your experience below if you have a story either way.
P.S. Comment: P.S. Ask your team what percentage of your current software they actually use.

I once took a job to replace the best person in the company.

He was already gone by the time I started. He had carried the whole client-delivery process in his head. No documents, no workflow, no handover. Years of knowledge had walked out the door with him.

I tried to rebuild what he knew from scratch while learning the job itself. Three months in, I had not caught up. I did not pass probation.

It was a hard moment. I had put most of my savings into a car to take that job.

Five years later I ran into the business owner. The business was gone, and he was working for someone else.

I did not get a clean ending to that chapter. But it taught me what I now build my practice around. A business that runs on one irreplaceable person has a single point of failure waiting for its moment.

The good news is this is fixable, and it starts small. Pick one process that only one person fully understands. Ask them to walk you through it while a colleague writes it down. Do that while the person is still in the building.

There's no coincidence, everything has a reason. That job is why I care so much about getting this right for others.

Which process in your business lives in just one person's head?
Comment: You do not need a big project to start. One process, one walkthrough, one written page. Do it this month, and the person who knows it best will usually enjoy sharing it.
P.S. Comment: P.S. Document it while the expert is happy and still around, not after.

The school bus picked me up thirty minutes before school started.

One morning I was not ready, and the bus left without me. I could not go to school, and I missed playing with my friends.

I was in primary school. I decided it would not happen twice.

From then on, I packed everything the night before. Books, uniform, water bottle. Five minutes before the bus arrived, I was at the door.

I still do it today. Every morning I brief myself, my team and the people around me. Every evening I debrief. What happened today, what could go better, what needs to be ready tomorrow.

The idea is simple. Prepare for the expected as much as humanly possible, so that when the unexpected arrives, I am dealing with only that. Not drowning in both.

When I look at the firms I advise, this is often the gap. They are not short of talent. They are short of a rhythm that brings the expected under control, so there is room to handle surprises.

A morning brief and an evening debrief cost fifteen minutes a day. They are how I manage risk and expectation, and they have been for most of my life.

How you do anything is how you do everything.

What is one small daily habit that keeps your week calm?
Comment: A brief and a debrief are free, and any team can start tomorrow. Even five minutes in the morning to name the top three things for the day makes a visible difference.
P.S. Comment: P.S. Debrief on what went well first. People share more honestly that way.

Stop buying another dashboard. Do this to your numbers first:

Dashboards are easy to like. They look sharp, they refresh, and they promise control. But a chart on a screen only reflects the number behind it. If that number has no clear home, the dashboard just displays the uncertainty more attractively.

It is common to find the same figure in three places with three different answers. The dashboard did not cause that. It showed it.

Before you add one more view, give each key number these four things:

1. A single source. One system where the number is created, not copied.
2. A named owner. One person who answers for it being right.
3. A written definition. What counts, what does not, and from when.
4. A decision it supports. If no decision depends on it, retire it.

Pick your five most important numbers and do this for each. It takes an afternoon.

After that, a dashboard becomes a multiplier. Your people spend their time acting on the number, not arguing about which one is right.

Good numbers, owned, defined and used. That is where control starts.

Which key number in your business has no clear owner right now?
Comment: Start with the number your board asks about most often. If it has a source, an owner, a definition and a decision attached, you are ahead of most firms.
P.S. Comment: P.S. Retiring unused numbers is the easiest win. Fewer numbers, better attention.

“Football is a game. Business is serious.”

Fair. But football taught me more about resilience than most business books.

Until the 90th minute, I still thought Bayern Munich were going to win that Champions League final. Then Solskjaer scored. It was "Fergie Time". Manchester United went on to win the Champions League and the treble that season.

That is the moment I understood what refusing to accept the scoreboard looks like, on a pitch or in a business.

Behind every club sit people in management, finance, facilities, logistics, coaching and matchday crews. Behind them sit processes for strategy and recruitment. And behind those sit systems that track player health, statistics, finances and fans. People, process and technology, all working as one.

Here is what it taught me.

Good leadership turns a mediocre performance into a win. Great leadership builds systems that keep winning while that leader is in charge. The greatest leader leaves a winning legacy that carries on through generations.

That is the standard I hold for the firms I work with. Not one good season. A structure that keeps going.

So here is my question. If your business were behind in the 90th minute, what structure would you rely on to turn it around?
Comment: I would love to hear your own lesson from another world, whether it is sport, family, music or travel. The best business ideas often come from somewhere else.
P.S. Comment: P.S. A comeback is exciting. A system that rarely needs one is better.
